what_it_does: In-memory computing (doing arithmetic inside the memory chip rather than moving data to a separate processor) is a promising way to save energy in AI chips, because moving data across a chip consumes far more power than the math itself. This work tackles a specific pain point: the activation functions — the nonlinear steps like ReLU (which simply zeroes out negative values) that neural networks need between their multiply-and-add layers. In conventional in-memory designs, getting a nonlinear result requires converting the analog in-memory signal to digital, running it through a standard processor, then converting back to analog — three steps that waste time and energy. The authors build a circuit that keeps everything in the time domain: information is encoded as the width of a pulse (a short electrical burst), and a small programmable network of resistive memory cells (RRAM — a type of memory that changes resistance when a voltage is applied) computes the nonlinear function directly in pulse-width form, so the data never has to leave the analog domain. They also introduce a training algorithm that adjusts which subset of reference pulses to use during learning, improving the approximation accuracy of the analog computation.
